factAnswerRaw: Structured query against the relational source
stem: A support-operations team wants an existing RAG assistant, built over troubleshooting prose, to also answer how many escalations occurred in a single sales region this quarter. The operations director must approve before rollout. Which mechanism should handle this query type?

opts.t: Add hybrid retrieval that fuses dense and lexical rankings over the troubleshooting prose to catch the region name
Route the question to a structured query against the relational incident data, outside the vector index
Summarize the most relevant retrieved escalation reports and give an approximate count from what was retrieved
Raise the retrieved chunk count so the model can tally matching incidents from the prose passages itself

whyRight: The request counts escalations within a region and a quarter, which is an aggregation over structured fields, not a similarity match. No amount of retrieval tuning answers a count; the relational source that already holds discrete incident records is the only mechanism that can compute it directly.

whyWrong.A: Hybrid retrieval fuses ranking signals for prose and identifiers, but a count is not a ranking problem; no fusion method returns a reliable tally of matching records.
whyWrong.C: An approximate count from whatever was retrieved is not a reliable answer to a 'how many' question; retrieval was never going to guarantee every matching record was found.
whyWrong.D: More retrieved passages still leave the model estimating a count from prose it can read, not from a complete, queryable set of records — accuracy is not guaranteed.

t1Clause: how many escalations occurred in a single sales region this quarter

factAnswerRaw: Reduce candidate width, or fund the stage by recovering latency elsewhere
stem: A retrieval pipeline for a support assistant finds the correct document consistently ranked eleventh among fifty candidates. Adding a reranking stage would push p95 latency past the 1,200ms SLA. Which change fixes the ranking problem without breaching that SLA?

opts.t: Add the reranking stage as designed, even though p95 latency will land past the stated 1,200ms SLA
Replace the retrieval mechanism, since the correct document is not reaching the candidate set
Cut the candidate width to five without reranking, so fewer documents are scored before the SLA check
Narrow the candidate width feeding the reranker, or recover latency elsewhere in the pipeline to fund the stage

whyRight: The document is already present at rank eleven, so the fix is ranking, not depth; reranking solves that but as specified would breach the SLA, so the width feeding the reranker must shrink, or latency must be recovered upstream, to keep the fix inside the stated budget.

whyWrong.A: Reranking is the right move for a document stuck at rank eleven, but shipping it while breaching the stated SLA trades away a real constraint instead of fitting inside it.
whyWrong.B: The stem states the document is consistently found at rank eleven among fifty candidates, so it is already in the set; the mechanism is not the fault here.
whyWrong.C: Narrowing candidates to five without reranking risks dropping the document the pipeline is already retrieving at rank eleven, discarding the very result the scenario needs kept.

t1Clause: would push p95 latency past the 1,200ms SLA

factAnswerRaw: Direct API from the orchestration layer, not a tool
stem: A regulated messaging workflow must run a disclosure check on every outbound message mentioning investment performance, with no exceptions the compliance office accepts. A proposal exposes the check as a callable tool after drafting. What should replace this design?

opts.t: Keep it as a tool, but log every drafted reply where the agent skipped the check for later review
Keep it as a tool and add a system-prompt rule instructing the agent to always call the check before sending
Call the check directly from the orchestration layer whenever a message references investment performance, outside the agent's discretion
Expose the check as a plain MCP tool, and let the agent judge on its own when disclosure applies

whyRight: The check is mandatory on every qualifying message with no exception the compliance office accepts, so its execution cannot depend on a model choosing to call it. A direct call from the orchestration layer makes the step deterministic and keeps it outside the agent's discretion entirely.

whyWrong.A: Logging a skipped check catches the miss after a reply is already drafted; the requirement is that the check always runs, not that skips are recorded for later review.
whyWrong.B: A prompt instruction to always call the check turns a hard requirement into something the model can still choose to skip, which is exactly the failure mode being fixed.
whyWrong.D: Letting the agent decide reintroduces the exact discretion the requirement rules out; that pattern fits when the model should judge whether to search, not a rule with no exceptions.

t1Clause: with no exceptions the compliance office accepts

factAnswerRaw: Investigate the index: completeness, chunk schema, embedding version, stale vectors
stem: A compliance team's document-QA system starts producing fluent, confident, wrong answers immediately following an overnight content sync. Cited clause numbers no longer match the quoted text, and retrieval scores dropped uniformly with no content edited. Select two.

opts.t: Lower the sampling temperature, since confident wrong answers usually indicate the model is hallucinating
Check for a partial re-index or a chunk-schema change that could explain the clause-number mismatch
Move the system to a newer, higher-capability generation model to improve overall answer quality
Check whether the embedding model version pinned to the index has drifted from the one used to build it

whyRight: The failure begins exactly at the sync, so the indexing layer is the suspect, not the model. A clause-number mismatch points to a schema or partial re-index; a uniform score drop with no content change points to embedding-version drift — both are re-index-layer causes worth checking first.

whyWrong.A: The degradation began precisely at the overnight content sync, an indexing event; that timing already rules out a pure model-behavior cause like sampling temperature as the explanation.
whyWrong.C: Swapping in a more capable model replaces a working component instead of investigating the one thing that actually changed: the index built during the sync.

t1Clause: immediately following an overnight content sync

stem: Retrieval precision has been falling as an engineering team steadily increases chunk size for more surrounding text, now averaging 1,800 tokens per chunk across 40,000 documents. Users still report answers missing context. What should change in the chunking approach?

opts.t: Reduce chunk size back down and prepend the document title and heading path to each chunk's text before embedding
Continue increasing chunk size so each chunk carries even more of the surrounding document text
Adjust chunk boundaries so no chunk ends mid-sentence or mid-clause, leaving size unchanged
Store the heading path in chunk metadata only, without changing the text that gets embedded

whyRight: Precision is falling because each embedding is being spread across more topics as chunks grow, not because chunks are missing content. Shrinking chunk size back down and prepending the title and heading path puts the missing context directly into the vector without diluting it.

whyWrong.B: The team is already growing chunks to add context and precision is dropping as a result; growing them further trades away the accuracy the pipeline needs to keep.
whyWrong.C: Boundary repair fixes chunks cut mid-idea; these chunks are already complete and merely ambiguous once pulled out of their surrounding heading structure.
whyWrong.D: Metadata is filterable but is not part of what gets embedded, so it does nothing to change which chunks are retrieved or how they rank.

t1Clause: Retrieval precision has been falling as an engineering team steadily increases chunk size

stem: A fraud-review agent calls five stable tools that rarely change, under a 300ms p95 latency budget that cannot absorb an extra model turn. A proposal adds a namespace-level index with on-demand expansion. What should happen instead?

opts.t: Add a namespace-level index with on-demand expansion, the pattern used for larger tool surfaces elsewhere
Load all five tools directly into the base context and skip the discovery step entirely
Drop the two least-used of the five tools so less loads on every request
Expose the five tools as a readable resource the agent can consult before deciding whether to act

whyRight: Five tools that rarely change is a small, stable surface, and the 300ms budget cannot absorb an extra model turn; that combination is exactly where loading everything up front beats progressive discovery, since the round-trip cost buys nothing this surface needs.

whyWrong.A: A namespace index earns its keep on a large surface where the round-trip is cheap relative to the tokens saved; here it adds latency the budget cannot spend.
whyWrong.C: Dropping tools the workflow still calls trades away required capability to solve a loading-strategy problem; the surface only has five tools, and all five are needed.
whyWrong.D: A resource is content the agent reads on its own initiative; these five capabilities must be invoked to act, and reclassifying them changes nothing about load time.

t1Clause: calls five stable tools that rarely change
